title: 12 Wake-up Calls That Every Leader Needs to Hear
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Framed deliberately as a set of hard truths, this piece argues that most team failures are leadership failures and that the leader must look in the mirror before looking anywhere else. The twelve calls cluster around accountability and trust: owning mistakes, taking blame while sharing credit, and treating an underperforming team as a verdict on one's own expectations, resources and culture. A second cluster distinguishes positional authority from earned leadership, insisting that a title makes someone a manager while their people make them a leader. The author also targets specific credibility-killers - playing favourites while preaching teamwork, micromanaging, and saying one thing while doing another. One of the more pointed claims is that a silent team is itself evidence of failed leadership, because silence means people do not feel safe to speak. Each call closes with do and don't guidance, and the whole list rests on a servant-leadership premise that the leader works for the team, not the reverse.
points: The opening call sets the frame: if a team misses deadlines or goals, the first diagnosis is the leader's own expectations, resources and culture, not the team members.
The author separates formal authority from leadership, arguing that respect and trust must be earned through conduct rather than conferred by a title.
Micromanagement is treated as a trust signal in reverse - a leader who does not trust the team gives the team little reason to trust the leader.
A silent team is read as a loud warning sign of missing psychological safety, with innovation and problem-solving stalling as a result.
The closing rule - take the blame and share the fame, with no exceptions - distils the piece's accountability-centred view of credibility.
quotes: If your team is underperforming, missing deadlines, or failing to meet goals, it’s a reflection of your leadership. Your role is to guide, support, and enable your team to succeed.
If you can’t handle feedback — especially the negative kind — you’re not ready to lead. Criticism, when taken constructively, is a tool for improvement.
Leadership isn’t given — it’s earned through your actions and the way you treat your people. Remember, your title may make you a manager, but it’s your team that makes you a leader.
This lack of trust can quickly undermine your credibility as a leader and erode the trust your team has in you. Effective leadership is about empowering your team, not controlling every detail.

When team members don’t feel safe to speak up, innovation stalls, problems go unresolved, and morale suffers. As a leader, it’s your responsibility to create an environment where open communication is not just encouraged but expected.

If you fail to own up to your mistakes, you undermine your integrity and erode your team's trust. Accountability is not just about accepting blame — it’s about demonstrating that you are committed to learning and improving.
When things go wrong, a true leader steps up and takes the blame. Conversely, when success is achieved, it’s important to give credit where it’s due and celebrate the team’s contributions.
